topics.verifiedDefinition: In JavaScript, 'var' is function-scoped and hoisted with an initial value of undefined, allowing re-declaration and reassignment. 'let' and 'const' are block-scoped, hoisted to the top of their enclosing block without initialization (residing in the Temporal Dead Zone until declared), and cannot be re-declared in the same scope. 'let' allows reassignment, while 'const' identifiers cannot be reassigned (though mutable object properties can still change).
keyConcepts: Function scope vs Block scope
Hoisting differences and initializations
Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) for let and const
Re-declaration vs Reassignment capabilities
Object/Array mutability with const
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must distinguish block vs function scope and not claim const creates deeply immutable data structures.

topics.verifiedDefinition: React Hooks (introduced in React 16.8) are functions that let functional components use state, lifecycle methods, and other React features without writing class components. They solve code reuse across components (custom hooks replace render props and HOCs) and prevent complex lifecycle duplication, adhering to the Rules of Hooks (only call at top level, only call from React functions).
keyConcepts: State and lifecycle access inside functional components
Elimination of class components and 'this' binding complexity
Stateful logic extraction and reuse via Custom Hooks
Rules of Hooks: Top-level invocation and React function caller restriction
Primary built-in hooks: useState, useEffect, useContext, useMemo, useCallback
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must identify that hooks enable functional components to have state and eliminate class lifecycle boilerplate.

topics.verifiedDefinition: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory lightweight JavaScript tree representation of the real DOM. When state or props change, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and executes a heuristic diffing algorithm (O(n) complexity) via the Fiber reconciliation engine to compute minimal real DOM mutations, batching updates to prevent expensive layout recalibration and repaints.
keyConcepts: In-memory representation of DOM tree nodes
Heuristic diffing algorithm (O(n) complexity)
Reconciliation process comparing previous and next trees
Fiber architecture for interruptible and prioritized rendering
Batched DOM updates minimizing browser layout thrashing
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must articulate that Virtual DOM is an in-memory abstraction and uses diffing to minimize real DOM mutations.

topics.verifiedDefinition: A closure is the combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment. In JavaScript, closures grant inner functions persistent access to an enclosing outer function's scope variables, even after the outer function has executed and returned.
keyConcepts: Lexical scoping and scope chain hierarchy
Inner function access to outer function variables
Memory persistence of closed-over lexical environment
Data privacy and encapsulation (module pattern)
Use cases: partial application, currying, event handlers, and memoization
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must state that inner functions retain access to outer function scope after the outer function finishes executing.

topics.verifiedDefinition: The JavaScript Event Loop is a single-threaded concurrency model that coordinates execution of synchronous code on the Call Stack and asynchronous callbacks from the Task Queue. When the Call Stack clears, the Event Loop first drains all callbacks in the Microtask Queue (Promises, queueMicrotask, process.nextTick) before executing the next Macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O events).
keyConcepts: Single-threaded execution with non-blocking I/O
Call Stack execution lifecycle
Microtask Queue (Promise reactions, nextTick) priority over Macrotask Queue
Macrotask Queue (setTimeout, I/O, UI rendering)
Role of Libuv in Node.js background thread pooling
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must mention Microtask priority over Macrotasks and explain non-blocking concurrency.

topics.verifiedDefinition: A Promise in JavaScript is an object representing the eventual completion (fulfillment) or failure (rejection) of an asynchronous operation, with three mutually exclusive states: pending, fulfilled, and rejected. 'async/await' is syntactic sugar built on top of Promises and Generators that allows asynchronous code to be written and read like synchronous code, using try/catch blocks for error handling.
keyConcepts: Promise states: Pending, Fulfilled, Rejected
Promise chaining and avoid callback hell
async/await as non-blocking syntactic sugar over Promises
Error handling via try/catch and .catch()
Promise concurrency methods: Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must accurately identify async/await as syntactic sugar over promises and detail the three promise states.

topics.verifiedDefinition: In Node.js, the event loop is powered by the C-based Libuv library. It operates across discrete phases: Timers (setTimeout/setInterval), Pending Callbacks (I/O errors), Idle/Prepare, Poll (retrieving new I/O events), Check (setImmediate callbacks), and Close Callbacks. Long compute operations should never block the event loop; CPU-intensive tasks are offloaded to Libuv thread pool or Worker Threads.
keyConcepts: Libuv event loop phases (Timers, Poll, Check, Close)
setImmediate vs process.nextTick priority order
Offloading expensive I/O to system kernel or thread pool
Avoid blocking the single main event thread
Worker threads and clustering for CPU workloads
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must recognize Libuv phases or non-blocking I/O principles without confusing Node with multi-threaded runtimes.

topics.verifiedDefinition: Node.js EventEmitter is a core module implementing the Observer pattern. It allows objects to emit named events that trigger registered listener functions synchronously in the sequence they were attached. Used widely in streams, HTTP servers, and sockets.
keyConcepts: Observer design pattern implementation
Synchronous execution order of event listeners
Handling error events to prevent process crashes
Memory leak safeguards (setMaxListeners / removeListener)
Decoupled publish-subscribe communication
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must describe observer/pub-sub pattern and synchronous invocation of listeners.

topics.verifiedDefinition: SQL databases are relational data stores with rigid tabular schemas, ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) transaction guarantees, and support complex joins, typically scaled vertically. NoSQL databases (document, key-value, column, graph) feature dynamic or schema-less data models, prioritize high throughput and horizontal partitioning (sharding) across clusters, often adhering to BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) properties.
keyConcepts: Relational tables with strict schemas vs Schema-less/flexible documents
ACID transactional guarantees vs BASE eventual consistency
Vertical scaling (compute/storage sizing) vs Horizontal scaling (sharding)
Complex SQL JOIN queries vs Denormalized embedded document models
Appropriate selection: structured transactional financial vs polymorphic large-scale telemetry data
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must distinguish relational vs non-relational, schema rigidity vs flexibility, and scaling strategies.

topics.verifiedDefinition: Representational State Transfer (REST) is an architectural style for networked systems based on stateless client-server communication using standard HTTP methods (GET for safe reads, POST for creation, PUT/PATCH for updates, DELETE for removals). Core constraints include stateless requests (every request contains complete auth and contextual state), resource-based URIs, uniform interfaces, and appropriate HTTP status codes (2xx success, 4xx client errors, 5xx server errors).
keyConcepts: Stateless client-server architecture
HTTP method semantics (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) and idempotency
Resource-oriented URI hierarchy (nouns over verbs)
Standardized HTTP status codes (200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500)
Standard representation formats (JSON, MIME types, cache headers)
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must emphasize statelessness, HTTP verbs mapping to CRUD, and resource URIs.

topics.verifiedDefinition: The CSS Box Model is a container design foundation that wraps around every HTML element. It consists of four concentric layers from inside to outside: Content area, Padding (space around content), Border (surrounding the padding), and Margin (transparent space outside the border separating neighboring elements). The 'box-sizing: border-box' property includes padding and border within the specified element width and height.
keyConcepts: Four layers: Content, Padding, Border, Margin
Difference between padding (inside border) and margin (outside border)
box-sizing: content-box (default, width excludes padding/border)
box-sizing: border-box (width includes padding and border, preventing layout overflow)
Margin collapsing behavior on vertical boundaries
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must list all 4 layers (content, padding, border, margin) and explain box-sizing: border-box.

topics.verifiedDefinition: The CAP Theorem states that in a distributed data store, you can only simultaneously provide at most two out of three guarantees: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every non-failing node returns a response), and Partition Tolerance (the system continues operating despite network message drops). Since network partitions are physically inevitable, distributed systems must trade off Consistency vs Availability (CP vs AP).
keyConcepts: Consistency (Strong linearizable vs Eventual)
Availability (Uptime and non-error responses)
Partition Tolerance (Resilience against network dropouts)
Inevitable CP vs AP architectural trade-offs
PACELC extension: latency vs consistency trade-offs when no partition exists
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must state that partition tolerance is mandatory in distributed systems, forcing CP vs AP tradeoff.

topics.verifiedDefinition: A database index is a data structure (commonly B-Trees or B+Trees) that improves data retrieval speed from O(N) full-table scans to O(log N) logarithmic searches, at the cost of additional disk storage space and write overhead during INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations as indexes must be rebuilt.
keyConcepts: B-Tree / B+Tree balanced hierarchical structures
Time complexity improvement (O(log N) vs O(N))
Primary clustered indexes vs Secondary unclustered indexes
Write penalty trade-off during row modifications
Composite index leftmost prefix rules
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must identify B-Tree structures, O(log N) speedups, and write performance penalty.

topics.verifiedDefinition: JSON Web Token (JWT) is an open standard (RFC 7519) consisting of Header, Payload, and Signature, used for stateless authentication. To guard against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), JWTs should be stored in HttpOnly, Secure cookies rather than localStorage. To guard against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), cookies should use SameSite=Strict/Lax policies or anti-CSRF challenge tokens.
keyConcepts: Three-part anatomy: Header, Payload, Cryptographic Signature
Stateless token-based authentication
HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags preventing XSS token exfiltration
SameSite cookie attributes and anti-CSRF token verification
Token expiration (exp claim) and sliding refresh rotation
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must specify 3 JWT parts and explain HttpOnly cookie protection against XSS.

topics.verifiedDefinition: Big O notation mathematically characterizes the worst-case upper bound of an algorithm's runtime or auxiliary memory usage as the input size N scales to infinity. Common complexity classes include Constant O(1), Logarithmic O(log N), Linear O(N), Linearithmic O(N log N), and Quadratic O(N^2).
keyConcepts: Upper bound worst-case asymptotic notation
Time vs Space memory complexity trade-offs
O(1) hash table average lookup vs O(N) worst-case collision
O(log N) divide-and-conquer binary search
O(N log N) comparison sort algorithms (Merge Sort, Quick Sort)
topics.antiHallucinationCheck: Must define asymptotic upper bound and cite standard complexity hierarchies.
